title: Chapter 13: The Elegant Flirt 3
content:
Chapter 13

Years later, whenever Wei Wuxian traced back the roots of his fractured relationship with Lan Wangji, he figured the blame lay squarely on those three months in Gusu when he and Jiang Cheng were fifteen.

The Gusu Lan Sect had an elder of towering renown named Lan Qiren, famous across the cultivation world for three definitive traits: he was pedantic, pigheaded, and he ran an ironclad boot camp that consistently churned out brilliant disciples. While the first two qualities made sensible people keep a cautious distance—or secretly despise him—the third had aristocratic parents practically tripping over themselves to ship their sons off to his lectures. Under his thumb, he’d shaped generations of model Lan heirs; even if you dumped a useless lump of trash into his classroom for a year or two, the kid was guaranteed to walk out looking like a respectable gentleman, or at least a civilized human being with immaculate table manners. Countless mothers and fathers had wept genuine tears of gratitude upon picking up their newly polished boys.

Hearing this, Wei Wuxian had deadpanned, “What, you mean I’m not civilized enough already?”

Jiang Cheng, possessing terrifying foresight, had countered, “You are guaranteed to go down as the single greatest stain on his entire teaching career.”

That year, alongside the boys from Yunmeng Jiang, scions from across the prominent clans had flooded in, packed off by parents dazzled by the Lan elder's reputation. At fifteen or sixteen, and hailing from families that traded seasonal courtesies, they all recognized each other even if they weren't particularly close. Everyone knew that despite not sharing the Jiang surname, Wei Wuxian was the son of Jiang Fengmian’s old friend and the Yunmeng Jiang Sect's Head Disciple—pampered and raised alongside the clan heir like a son of the house. Besides, teenage boys cared infinitely less about pedigree and bloodlines than their stuffy elders did. Within minutes, the ice was shattered, everyone slapping shoulders and trading fraternal nicknames.

One of the boys leaned in, curious. “Lotus Pier’s gotta be a hundred times more fun than this tomb, right?”

Wei Wuxian flashed an easy grin. “Fun is whatever you make of it. But I’ll tell you this: we sure don’t have half these absurd rules, and we definitely don’t roll out of bed at the crack of dawn.”

The Gusu Lan Sect operated on a merciless schedule: rise at five in the morning, sleep at nine at night, sharp.

Another boy pressed, “Wait, so when do you guys get up? What do you even do all day?”

Jiang Cheng scoffed. “Him? He rolls out of bed at nine in the morning and crashes at one past midnight. And when he's awake, does he meditate or drill his sword forms? Hell no. He’s out rowing boats, swimming, stealing lotus pods, and shooting wild pheasants.”

Wei Wuxian countered smoothly, “And no matter how many pheasants I bag, I'm still top of the class.”

A starry-eyed boy raised a fist. “That's it. Next year I'm transferring to Yunmeng! Nobody try to stop me!”

A cold bucket of reality splashed over his head: “Nobody’s going to stop you. Your big brother will just break your legs.”

The boy instantly wilted. That was Nie Huaisang, the second young master of the Qinghe Nie Sect. His elder brother, Nie Mingjue, ruled the clan with an iron fist, commanding immense awe across the cultivation sects. Though born of different mothers, the brothers shared a fierce bond; Nie Mingjue was impossibly strict with the kid, micromanaging his studies with hawkish scrutiny. Nie Huaisang idolized his brother, sure, but he lived in absolute terror of the man asking about his grades.

Wei Wuxian piped up, “To be fair, Gusu isn't all that bad.”

Nie Huaisang leaned across, speaking in hushed, dead-serious tones. “Brother Wei, take some heartfelt advice from me. The Cloud Recesses is not Lotus Pier. Now that you’re in Gusu, memorize this rule: there is one person you must never, ever provoke.”

Wei Wuxian blinked. “Who? Lan Qiren?”

“Not the old man,” Nie Huaisang whispered. “The one you have to watch out for is his prize pupil. A guy named Lan Zhan.”

Wei Wuxian tilted his head. “Lan Zhan? As in, the Twin Jades of Lan’s Lan Zhan? Lan Wangji?”

The two sons of the current Gusu Lan Sect Leader, Lan Huan and Lan Zhan, had long carried the illustrious moniker of the Twin Jades of Lan. Ever since they crossed fourteen, clan elders across the world had held them up as demigods, using them as living measuring sticks to berate their own sons. Their reputation preceded them everywhere.

Nie Huaisang shuddered. “Who else could it be? Him! Man, he’s our age, but he doesn't have a single drop of youthful blood in his veins. He’s rigid, icy, and stricter than his own uncle—if you can believe that.”

Wei Wuxian let out a thoughtfuloh. “Wait. Is he that exceptionally pretty boy?”

Jiang Cheng snorted. “It’s the Gusu Lan Sect. You think they let ugly people in? Their clan won't even accept disciples with crooked noses. Go on, I dare you to find a single plain face in this entire mountain.”

“No, I meanunusuallypretty,” Wei Wuxian insisted, gesturing around his own temple. “Dressed in head-to-toe white, wearing a forehead ribbon, with an iced-silver sword slung across his back. Drop-dead gorgeous, but wearing a scowl so stiff you’d think he was attending his own funeral.”

Nie Huaisang’s jaw slacked. “...That's him! Exactly him!” He paused, blinking. “Wait, but he was in secluded meditation until recently, and you only arrived yesterday. When did you see him?”

“Last night.”

“Last ni—last night?!” Jiang Cheng stared at him, flabbergasted. “The Cloud Recesses has a strict curfew! Where did you run into him? How come I didn't know about this?”

Wei Wuxian pointed lazily toward the courtyard. “Up there.”

He was pointing directly at a soaring roof ledge.

The boys fell completely mute. A migraine exploded behind Jiang Cheng’s eyes. He ground his teeth, hissing, “You haven't been here a full day and you’re already kicking up trouble?! What happened?”

Wei Wuxian grinned, entirely unrepentant. “Nothing dramatic! Remember that tavern selling Emperor’s Smile we passed on the way in? I was tossing and turning last night, couldn't take it anymore, so I slipped down the mountain into town and hauled two jars back. You can't get that vintage in Yunmeng, you know.”

Jiang Cheng snapped, “Where's the wine now?”

“Well, I’d just vaulted the perimeter wall,” Wei Wuxian explained. “I didn't even have my second foot planted inside before he caught me red-handed.”

One of the boys winced. “Brother Wei, that’s rotten luck. He must have just broken seclusion and taken up the night patrol. You walked right into the tiger's jaws.”

Jiang Cheng rubbed his temples. “Disciples who return after hours aren't permitted entry until seven in the morning. How the hell did he let you in?”

Wei Wuxian shrugged. “He didn't! The guy insisted I pull my leg back over the wall. I asked him how the hell I was supposed to do that, and the next second, he floated up onto the tiles light as a feather, demanding to know what I had in my hands.”

Jiang Cheng felt his stomach drop. “...And you told him?”

“Of course! I said, ‘It’s Emperor’s Smile! How about I split a jar with you and you pretend you never saw me?’”

Jiang Cheng pinched the bridge of his nose, letting out a soul-weary sigh. “...Alcohol is strictly forbidden in the Cloud Recesses. You just handed him a confession.”

“That’s word-for-word what he told me!” Wei Wuxian laughed. “So I asked, ‘Why don’t you just tell me what your clandoesn'tforbid?’ That seemed to tick him off, because he told me to go read the Wall of Discipline. Seriously, who’s going to read over three thousand rules carved in ancient seal script? Did you read it? Did you? Exactly, nobody reads that! What was he getting so worked up about?”

“Right?!” The surrounding boys chimed in, nodding violently as they commiserated over the Cloud Recesses’ nightmarish rulebook. “Who has three thousand rules without repeating themselves?! ‘No killing within the grounds, no private brawling, no promiscuity, no nighttime wandering, no clamoring, no running’—fine, whatever! But who the hell bans ‘no unprovoked smirking, no slouching, and no eating more than three bowls of rice’?!”

Wei Wuxian suddenly perked up. “Wait. Private brawling is banned too?”

Jiang Cheng froze. “...Yes. Don't you dare tell me you fought him.”

“We did,” Wei Wuxian admitted breezily. “And one of my jars got knocked off the roof.”

A collective groan rippled through the teenagers, boys smacking their thighs in tragic mourning for the wasted vintage.

Seeing the situation couldn't possibly get any worse, Jiang Cheng’s focus derailed entirely. “You brought two jars. Where’s the other one?”

“Drank it.”

“Where?!”

“Right in front of his face. I told him, ‘Fine, if alcohol is banned inside the Cloud Recesses, then as long as I don't cross the threshold and drink it while perched on the outer wall, I’m technically not breaking the rules, right?’ And then I chugged the whole jar right before his eyes.”

Jiang Cheng’s voice shook. “...And then?”

“And then we started swinging.”

Nie Huaisang stared at him in utter awe. “Brother Wei. You have a death wish.”

Wei Wuxian clicked his tongue. “Lan Zhan’s sword work is remarkably good, actually.”

“You are a dead man, Brother Wei!” Nie Huaisang whisper-shrieked. “Lan Zhan has never taken a loss like that in his life. He’s definitely got his eye on you now! You’d better watch your back—even though he doesn’t attend these lectures with us, he’s the one in charge of clan punishments!”

Wei Wuxian waved a hand dismissively. “What's there to sweat? Isn't Lan Zhan supposed to be some legendary child prodigy? With that kind of freakish intellect, his uncle's curriculum must be ancient history to him. He spends half his life locked in secluded meditation—where would he find the time to breathe down my neck? I—”

Before he could finish digging his grave, the group turned the corner past an open lattice wall.

Sitting in pristine, rigid posture inside the Orchid Room was a youth clad in immaculate white. His long black hair was swept neatly beneath a cloud-patterned ribbon, his entire presence draped in an aura of winter frost. He lifted his head, sweeping a glacial glare across the doorway.

A dozen teenage mouths instantly slammed shut, looking as though they’d been struck with a collective Silence Spell. Filing into the lecture hall without a peep, they quietly claimed their desks, silently leaving a wide, barren DMZ of empty space around Lan Wangji’s seat.

Jiang Cheng clapped a heavy hand on Wei Wuxian’s shoulder, murmuring under his breath, “He’s got his eye on you. May the gods have mercy on your soul.”

Wei Wuxian tilted his head, catching a clean view of Lan Wangji’s profile. Fine, sweeping lashes, an impossibly elegant silhouette, sitting with unyielding, textbook perfection as he stared dead ahead. Wei Wuxian opened his mouth, toying with the idea of tossing out a greeting, when Lan Qiren swept into the hall.

Lan Qiren was tall, gaunt, and as stiff as a pine. While he sported a trim, black goatee, he was hardly old; keeping with the Gusu Lan tradition of producing exceptional beauties, he wasn't unsightly by any stretch. Unfortunately, the pedantic, sour aura clinging to his skin made calling him an old coot feel completely natural. He strode in brandishing a heavy parchment scroll, letting it unfurl across the floorboards in a dramatic flourish, and began reading the Lan Clan rules out loud from the top.

Every boy in the room turned a sickly shade of green.

Bored out of his skull, Wei Wuxian’s gaze began to drift, eventually settling back on the side of Lan Wangji’s face. Watching the boy listen with deep, unironic reverence, Wei Wuxian felt a bizarre pang of admiration:To listen to garbage this boring with that much focus—the guy’s an absolute monster!

Without warning, Lan Qiren slammed the scroll down onto his lectern, sneering coldly. “Carved into the mountain rock, yet nobody bothers to read it. That is why I am reciting every single clause aloud—to ensure none of you can plead ignorance when you transgress. Yet even now, someone dares to daydream. Fine. Let us see how well you handle real questions.”

While that reprimand could easily apply to every soul in the room, Wei Wuxian had a visceral gut feeling it was aimed directly at his forehead.

Sure enough, the elder barked: “Wei Ying.”

Wei Wuxian perked up. “Here.”

“Tell me: are fiends, demons, ghosts, and monsters the same entity?”

Wei Wuxian offered an easy smile. “They are not.”

“Why not? How do you distinguish them?”

“Fiends are formed from non-human living beings; demons are formed from living humans; ghosts are formed from deceased humans; and monsters are formed from non-human inanimate objects.”

“The line between 'fiend' and 'monster' is easily blurred. Provide an example to differentiate them.”

“Simple enough.” Wei Wuxian gestured through the lattice window toward a lush, sprawling tree outside. “Take that living tree: if it absorbs the scholarly essence of these halls over a century, develops spiritual sentience, and begins causing mischief, it is classified as a 'fiend.' But if I take a woodcutter’s axe, chop it down at the trunk, and leave behind a dead stump that later attains sentience, it becomes a 'monster.'”

Lan Qiren pressed, “What was the ancestral trade of the Qinghe Nie Sect?”

“Butchers.”

“The crest of the Lanling Jin Sect is the white peony. Which specific variety?”

“Sparks Amidst Snow.”

“Who was the first in the cultivation world to elevate the clan over the sect, ushering in the age of hereditary houses?”

“The founding ancestor of the Qishan Wen Sect, Wen Mao.”

Wei Wuxian tossed the answers back without missing a beat, leaving the surrounding boys riding a rollercoaster of vicarious nerves. Relieved that he wasn't tripping up, they silently prayed he’d keep the streak alive so the old coot wouldn't pivot and pick on them.

Lan Qiren stroked his beard coldly. “As a disciple of the Yunmeng Jiang Sect, you should have these fundamentals committed to memory anyway; getting them right is hardly cause for smugness. Let me pose another scenario: there exists an executioner with a full family—parents, a wife, and children. In his lifetime, he beheaded over a hundred criminals. He later dies a violent death in the public market, his corpse left exposed to the elements for seven days. Choked by accumulated resentment, he returns to cause bloody havoc. How do you handle it?”

This time, Wei Wuxian didn't shoot back an answer.

Watching him pause, the other disciples assumed he’d finally hit a wall, shifting uncomfortably in their seats. Lan Qiren snapped, “What are you all gawking at him for? Use your own heads! And keep your hands off the textbooks!”

The boys jerked their fingers back from their desks, dread mounting. Dying violently in a public market, left rotting for seven days—that was the recipe for a catastrophic fierce corpse, notoriously impossible to exorcise. Everyone silently prayed the old man’s finger wouldn't point their way.

Seeing Wei Wuxian standing in silence, seemingly lost in thought, Lan Qiren turned his gaze away. “Wangji. Enlighten him. How is it handled?”
